name: TSC2007IPWR
title: TSC2007: 1.2 V to 3.6 V, 12-bit nanopower 4-wire resistive touch screen controller with I2C interface
summary: A controller for 4-wire resistive touch panels that runs from a single 1.2 V to 3.6 V supply, which is also the converter reference. It drives the panel plates through internal switches, converts X, Y and the two pressure readings Z1 and Z2 with a ratiometric 12-bit or 8-bit SAR converter, and also measures an auxiliary input and an on-chip temperature diode. By default each result is the median-and-average of seven conversions, so the host reads one filtered value over an I2C slave port that works in standard, fast and high-speed modes (to 3.4 MHz). A buffered PENIRQ output with a 50 kΩ or 90 kΩ internal pull-up flags a touch. It comes in a 16-pin TSSOP (PW) and a 12-ball 1.5 mm × 2 mm WCSP (YZG), for -40 °C to +85 °C.
key_figures: 12 bits or 8 bits, programmable; 11 bits no missing codes
32.24 µA typ at 1.2 V, 39.31 µA at 1.8 V, 53.32 µA at 2.7 V (12-bit fast mode, 8.2 kHz equivalent rate)
up to 20 kHz (8-bit) or 10 kHz (12-bit) effective
standard 100 kHz, fast 400 kHz, high-speed 1.7 MHz and 3.4 MHz; address 10010 A1 A0
±8 kV HBM, ±1 kV CDM; ±25 kV air and ±15 kV contact (IEC 61000-4-2) on X+, X-, Y+, Y-

notes: All twelve orderables are active, in production and RoHS compliant.
An automotive-qualified version is listed as TSC2007-Q1.

circuits.title: Typical circuit configuration
circuits.description: A 1.8 V rail feeds VDD/REF directly, so the supply is also the converter reference; 1 µF and 0.1 µF capacitors decouple it to ground. The four panel electrodes go straight to X+, X-, Y+ and Y- with no other parts. PENIRQ goes to a GPIO on the host as its touch interrupt, and SDA and SCL run to the host's I2C port, each pulled up to the 1.8 V rail through 1.2 kΩ. AUX takes an outside analog signal. GND returns to ground.

notes: A1 and A0 carry no connection in this circuit; they set the two low bits of the slave address, and each is tied to VDD/REF or GND.

operation.text: Panel drivers and an input multiplexer feed a SAR converter; a preprocessing block filters the results; an internal clock runs the state machines and the converter; an I2C slave port carries commands and data. Every function is selected by writing one command byte to an internal register. No outside parts are needed beyond decoupling and the bus pull-ups.

The panel has two transparent resistive layers held apart by spacers. To read Y, the Y+ and Y- drivers put the supply across the Y layer and the converter samples the voltage that a touch passes to X+; X is read the same way with the X drivers on and the voltage taken from Y+. The converter's high input impedance means the sense lead's resistance does not enter the result.

Pressure is found as a touch resistance, from the two cross-panel readings Z1 and Z2 plus X and the X-plate resistance, or from Z1 plus X, Y and both plate resistances (the touch-resistance equations). Eight-bit resolution is often enough for this reading.

When a panel is pressed its voltage rings and then settles, and capacitors added across the panel to filter LCD or backlight noise lengthen the settling, which shows up as gain error. The driver-only commands ('1000', '1001', '1010') turn the drivers on without converting, so the panel can settle before the conversion command is sent. Usually the time to send a command over I2C is long enough.

The reference is the voltage on VDD/REF, so the reference range is the supply range, 1.2 V to 3.6 V. Panel measurements use a differential reference: +REF and -REF connect to the driven plate's two ends, which makes the reading ratiometric and cancels the drop across the driver switches. Single-ended reference mode is not supported for panel readings; TEMP and AUX are converted single-ended.

M = 0 selects 12 bits, M = 1 selects 8 bits. In 8-bit mode the converter clock is about 4 MHz instead of about 2 MHz, each conversion is four bits shorter, and the result fits in one data byte, which saves time and power. Output data are straight binary.

Two on-chip diodes are measured. TEMP1 alone reads about 580 mV at +25 °C with 10 µA, falling 2.1 mV/°C; its absolute value varies by a few millivolts, so it is calibrated once at a known temperature, after which one reading gives 0.35 °C/LSB resolution (1 LSB = 732 µV at VREF = 3.0 V). The differential method also converts TEMP2, whose diode has 91 times the resistance of TEMP1, and computes temperature from the difference without calibration, at lower resolution. Both readings use the same acquisition timing as the other channels. At VDD = 1.8 V, TEMP2 reads 94.2 mV above TEMP1 at -40 °C and 137.5 mV above it at +85 °C.

PENIRQ is pulled up inside through RIRQ, 50 kΩ by default or 90 kΩ after setup command '1011' with data '0001' ('0000' returns it to 50 kΩ). In power-down with PD0 = 0 the Y- driver is on to ground and X+ is tied to the pen-detect circuit, so a touch pulls X+ and PENIRQ low. During X, Y and Z measurements, and during the driver-only commands, X+ is disconnected from the detector and PENIRQ is held low whatever PD0 is. A command with PD0 = 1 leaves pen detect off until a command with PD0 = 0 is written. Pen detect is also off from the write-address acknowledge until the end of the conversion, about 100 µs (12-bit) or 50 µs (8-bit) after the STOP or START that follows the command; the host should mask the PENIRQ interrupt while it writes to the part.

Each result is formed from seven conversions: they are sorted and the middle three are averaged. The filter acts on every input (X, Y, Z, TEMP1, TEMP2, AUX). Setting bit D1 of the setup command bypasses it to shorten the conversion time.

PD1-PD0 choose the state after the current command: 00 powers down between cycles with PENIRQ enabled; 01 and 11 keep the converter on with PENIRQ disabled; 10 turns the converter off with PENIRQ enabled. PD0 = 0 gives the lowest consumption; PD0 = 1 keeps the panel drivers on after each conversion, for back-to-back readings. Right after power-up a command with PD1 = PD0 = 0 must be sent to put the part in its lowest power state.

The part is an I2C slave on open-drain SDA and SCL and works in standard (100 kHz), fast (400 kHz) and high-speed (1.7 MHz or 3.4 MHz) modes, as slave receiver or slave transmitter. For high-speed mode the SCL pull-up must be an active (current-source) pull-up; the master sends the master code 00001xxx in F/S mode, gets no acknowledge, then a repeated START switches to Hs mode until the next STOP. In Hs mode the part may stretch SCL low until its result is in the shift register.

The 7-bit address is 10010 followed by the levels on A1 and A0, so up to four parts can share one bus. A1 and A0 are read with every address byte, are tied to VDD/REF or GND, and are also sampled at power-on reset. The address is latched on the SCL falling edge after the R/W bit.

The master sends the address with R/W = 0, the part acknowledges, the master sends the command byte, the part acknowledges again, and a STOP or repeated START ends the cycle. More command bytes before that STOP are not acknowledged. The input channel is chosen when C3-C0 arrive; acquisition starts on the SCL falling edge after C0 is latched and lasts until the STOP or repeated START, then conversion begins at once. Panel drivers stay on through the conversion of an X, Y or Z reading.

The master sends the address with R/W = 1; after the acknowledge the part returns D11-D4, then, after the master's acknowledge, D3-D0 followed by four zeros. The master ends with a not-acknowledge; acknowledging the second byte returns FFh. This holds in 8-bit and 12-bit modes. For full 12-bit performance the bus should be idle during conversion, and the master should wait at least 10 µs before reading.

The converter samples at up to 200 kSPS inside, but each filtered result needs seven conversions and the bus transfer, so the effective rate across I2C is about 20 kSPS at 8 bits and 10 kSPS at 12 bits. A conversion takes 19 CCLK at 12 bits and 16 CCLK at 8 bits; the nominal 4 MHz clock runs 3.66 MHz to 3.82 MHz, and 3.19 MHz at VDD = 1.2 V. A 12-bit result costs 49 SCL cycles (20 write, 29 read) and 148 CCLK; an 8-bit result costs 40 SCL cycles (20 write, 20 read) and 127 CCLK.

An internal power-on reset sets the default state and samples A1 and A0. It works from the shape of the supply ramp, so VDD must fall at no less than 2 kV/s, stay at 0 V for at least 1.2 s (-40 °C to +85 °C) or 0.3 s (-20 °C to +85 °C), and rise at no less than 12 kV/s; the ramps are taken between 0.3 V and 0.9 V.

The SAR converter is sensitive to glitches on supply, reference, ground and digital inputs just before each bit decision. Place a 0.1 µF ceramic capacitor as close to the part as possible, and add 1 µF to 10 µF when the supply connection has high impedance. Supply noise and ripple pass straight into the result because VDD/REF is the reference. Keep active traces from under any pin marked VOID unless a ground or power plane shields them. Return GND to a clean, ideally analog, ground away from the microcontroller's ground point, by its own trace to the supply entry if needed. Keep the panel connection short and solid, since loose contacts add error as they flex. Against LCD noise, a panel with a grounded bottom metal layer helps, and so do capacitors from X+, X-, Y+ and Y- to ground, at the cost of longer settling.
The panel pins X+, X-, Y+ and Y- withstand ±25 kV air-gap and ±15 kV contact discharge (IEC 61000-4-2); the part is rated ±8 kV HBM and ±1 kV CDM.
